items.question: How do you think about how much control to give an AI model over your computer?
items.object: Giving AI models control of a user's computer
items.answer: I think it'd be great if the model could control my computer for sure, but in some sense there's a reason we don't go hog wild and say, "Oh yes, here's the keys to the kingdom. Have at it." There are still asymmetric costs to the time you can save and the types of errors you can make. So we're trying to iteratively deploy these things and try them out and figure out where are they reliable and where are they not, because if you did just let the model control your computer, it could do some cool stuff, I have no doubt. But do I trust it to respond to all of the random emails that Brandon sends me? Actually, maybe for that task it doesn't require that much intelligence. But more generally, do I trust it to do everything I'm doing? Some things, and I'm sure that set of things will be bigger tomorrow than it was yesterday. But I think part of this is we limit the affordances and keep it a little bit in the sandbox, just out of caution, so that you don't send some crazy email to your boss or delete all your texts or delete your hard drive or something.

The response presents iterative deployment as a way to discover which computer tasks an AI can perform reliably.

items.question: How do you think about environmental uncertainty when assessing the difficulty of tasks for AI models?
items.object: Environmental uncertainty as a factor in AI task difficulty
items.answer: I mean, I don't know if there's one organizing framework. I think there are a few factors, at least, that I think about in the very, very grand scheme of things. How much, in order to solve this task, do I have to wrestle with uncertainty in the environment? For some things where it's purely fact, like, "Who was the first president of the United States?" there's zero environment I need to interact with to reach the answer to this question correctly. I just need to remember the answer and say the answer.

items.question: How do you think about what makes tasks involving external environments hard for AI models?
items.object: The difficulty of AI tasks involving external environments
items.answer:
If I want you to write some code that solves some problem, now I have to deal with a little bit of not purely internal model stuff, but also, okay, I need to execute the code, and that code execution environment is maybe more complicated than my model can memorize internally. So I have to do a little bit of writing code and then executing it and making sure it does what I thought it did, and then testing it, and then giving it to the user. You can't just recall the answer and give it to the user. You have to test something and run an experiment in the world and then wait for the result of that experiment. The more you have to do that, the more uncertain the results of those experiments. In some sense, that's one of the core attributes of what makes the tasks hard.

And I think another is how simulatable they are. Stuff that is really bottlenecked by time, the physical world, is also just harder than stuff that we can simulate really well. It's not a coincidence that so many people are interested in coding and coding agents, and that robotics is hard and slower. I used to work on robotics, and it's frustrating in a lot of ways. I think both how much of the external environment do you have to deal with and how much do you have to wrestle with the unavoidable slowness of the real world are two dimensions that I sort of think about.

The response identifies the extent of required interaction with an external environment as a dimension of task difficulty.

items.question: How do you think training AI models to cooperate with each other could prepare them to collaborate with people?
items.object: Multi-agent reinforcement learning as preparation for collaboration with humans
items.answer: My spicy take on that is, I don't know, 03 in some sense is already kind of simulating what it'd be like for a single person to do something with a browser or something like that. Train two of them together, so that you'd have two people interacting with each other, and there's no reason you can't scale all this up so that models are trained to be really good at cooperating with each other. There's a lot of already existing literature on multi-agent RL, and if you want the model to be good at something like collaborating with a bunch of people, maybe a not-too-bad starting point is making it good at collaborating with other models.
quotes: My spicy take on that is, I don't know, 03 in some sense is already kind of simulating what it'd be like for a single person to do something with a browser or something like that.

Train two of them together, so that you'd have two people interacting with each other, and there's no reason you can't scale all this up so that models are trained to be really good at cooperating with each other.

rubrics.text: The response proposes jointly training multiple AI agents as a way to simulate interactions among multiple people.
The response suggests that training AI models to collaborate with other models could be a starting point for training them to collaborate with people.

items.question: How do you think about training AI models interactively with human intervention?
items.object: Interactive model training with human intervention
items.answer:
Sometimes I see our models training and I'm like, "What are you doing? You're taking forever to figure this out." I actually think it would be really fun if you could train models in an interactive way. Forget about just test time, but I think it'd be really neat to train them to do something like that, be able to intervene when it makes sense. More me being able to tell the model, "Cut it out," in the middle of its chain of thought and it being able to learn from that on the fly, I think would be great.

I do think this is the intersection of these two things, where it's both a point of contact with the external environment that can be very high uncertainty—humans can be very unpredictable in some cases—and it's sort of limited by the tick of time in the real world if you want to deal with actual humans. Humans have a fixed clock cycle in their head. So, if you want to do this in the literal sense, it's hard, and scaling it up and making it work well is not obvious how to do.

items.question: How do you view the difficulty of human collaboration compared with writing code in a research project?
items.answer: But the human part is important. I think in any research project, my interactions with Brandon are the hardest part of the project. Writing the code, that's the easy part.
quotes: But the human part is important. I think in any research project, my interactions with Brandon are the hardest part of the project. Writing the code, that's the easy part.
